newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban urge early start to Afghan gas project.
newsitem.headline: Taleban urge early start to Afghan gas project.

text.p: A senior Taleban official on Wednesday urged an early start to a proposed $2.5-billion pipeline to carry gas from Central Asia to Pakistan via Afghanistan.

"It is the right time. They should not lose more time because they have already waited a long time and the Iranians are using the situation in their favour," the Taleban's acting deputy Foreign Minister Sher Abbas Stanakzai told journalists.

As Stanakzai spoke, a conference in the Turkmen capital of Ashgabat discussed ways of exporting Central Asia's mineral resources to the outside world. The Taleban were not invited to the Economic Cooperation Organisation conference, which groups 10 central and southeast Asian countries.
Afghanistan's seat was occupied by President Burhanuddin Rabbani, whom the Taleban ousted from Kabul last September.

Stanakzai said no final agreement had been signed with either of the two leading consortia, one led by Unocal of the United States and Delta Oil of Saudi Arabia, and the other by Argentine energy independent Bridas

Both proposed pipelines run down the western side of Afghanistan before turning east to connect with Pakistan's network. The pipeline is expected to have a capacity of 20 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas a year.
Stanakzai said the major determining factors for the Taleban would be the advantages that accrued to Afghanistan and who started work first.
"We have told (Unocal and Bridas) that we will sign a final agreement with the company that can give us more advantages and who will sooner start their work," Stanakzai said.
A Bridas representative said in Kabul on May 4 that they hoped to sign a deal before the end of the month.
"The final agreement is under discussion and we hope to sign by the end of the month," Mario Lopez Olaciregui, managing director of Bridas International Ltd, told Reuters.
Stanakzai said there was a possibility that his administration would sign deals with both parties.
"There will be no problem if Bridas starts their work and Unocal starts their own pipeline beside them," he said.
Stanakzai dismissed opposition threats to disrupt the building and operation of the pipeline.

"(The opposition) have threatened to attack the pipeline, but they cannot attack because if they do they will go against the wishes of the Afghan people, and I think that the few people who are supporting them will leave them," he said.
Stanakzai said the proposed route was entirely under Taleban control and the opposition did not present a great threat.

"In those areas that the pipeline is supposed to go through, peace is being maintained and they can work peacefully. The opposition are weakened and we do not think that they have the strength to come back," he said.
"The (Taleban) government is fully aware of the situation and we are quite capable. We will not let anybody harm this project."
The Taleban control almost two-thirds of Afghanistan but face an opposition alliance that includes the ousted government in the northeast of the country.
The Taleban have yet to be recognised as Afghanistan's legitimate government by any country or international body.
